tone_statements.citation: Luo, Yongxian. 2008. Zhuang. In A. V. N. Diller, J. A. Edmondson & Y. Luo (eds), The Tai-Kadai Languages (Routledge Language Family Series), 317-377. London: Routledge.
tone_statements.quote: Like the initials, tonal variations are noticeable. The tonal pitches of a number of dialects differ substantially from those of Wuming, the speech of Standard Zhuang. Table 9.2-4 contrasts the tones among six Zhuang dialects.* TABLE 9.2-4: TONE CONTRAST IN SIX ZHUANG DIALECTS GLOSS / PHONETICS | ‘dog’ |‘rice field ‘grow’ ‘horse’ ‘soak’ | ‘river’ ma na ma ma ma ta Wuming 24 31 55 42 35 33 … 4 The numerics in the box indicate the tonal pitch using Chao’s 5-scale notation.

Adams & Thomas John Hudak (eds), Papers from the Second Annual Meeting of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society (SEALS II, 1992), 147-185. Tempe: Arizona State University, Program for Southeast Asian Studies.
tone_statements.quote: Thus, A -> 1, 2; B -> 5,6; C -> 3, 4; DS -> 7, 8; and DL -> 7, 8 (vowel length distinguishes these from DS). ... 7.1. Northern Zhuang tonal development. Northern Zhuang tone systems are generally very close to the paradigmatic 5X2 profile that results from splitting according to the Voiced-Low Principle (Brown 1975) having the top three boxes in each column in the high tone category and bottom box in the low tone category. This standard system, which I will call Type 1 is found at very many NZ locations. Type 1 Pure voiced-low splitting exceptionless at points (4-8, 12-22, 24-33), represented by Yongfu.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 165-166, section 7 and 7.1 (also p. 164 on no tonal flip-flop; p. 171 Wuming-Daxin A-tone table)
